title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation fraud in which AI-generated content was used to fabricate a financial interview involving two real, named public figures. The fake article presented a non-existent conversation as factual journalism, lending false credibility to an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The failure occurred entirely outside any legitimate AI deployment, as scammers used AI tools to produce deceptive content rather than a company misdeploying its own product.

The scale reported by the regulator indicates this is not an isolated case. ASIC describes scammers building layered networks of fake news articles, websites, and testimonials, each element reinforcing the others. That layering means a single check against one piece of content is insufficient, because the surrounding ecosystem is also fabricated. Catching this kind of fraud requires cross-referencing claimed interviews against source outlets directly and verifying licence numbers through official registers, steps that place the detection burden on the consumer rather than on any platform gatekeeping the content.

What is not established is whether any specific AI tool or company is responsible for producing the fake material, and ASIC's warnings constitute a regulatory alert rather than findings of liability against any identified party.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featured a fabricated interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock discussing Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The article never happened and was generated using artificial intelligence. This represents a growing type of scam that Australian Securities and Investments Commission says is becoming more prevalent and sophisticated due to advances in AI technology.

ASIC's latest research reveals investment scams are surging, with the regulator removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. Phishing scams jumped 279 percent while fake investment platforms increased 151 percent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, politician Pauline Hanson, businessman Dick Smith, and billionaire Gina Rinehart are among the most commonly impersonated figures. Scammers build elaborate networks of fake news articles, websites, and testimonials to deceive consumers. ASIC advises people to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers independently before investing and to check company details against ASIC's public registers.
